name: Aisha Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead a carpentry crew building timber porch roofs on housing sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and know how to brace an awkward roof, but our small builder pays me below the usual carpenter rate. I like seeing the roof sit square; gaps between contracts wear the household down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works changing grocery shifts and our children are grown. We rent and have about three weeks of expenses saved, with few similar builders nearby. I use AI every day for timber counts and schedules, then check the wall myself; retirement is in sight, but I hope to work to about 69 if the money and my health allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can tidy a timber order, but the team still has to brace a real porch roof. I'd keep using my daily tool for the list and getting the work built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a lead carpenter yet our small builder pays below the usual rate, and my partner's grocery shifts change week to week. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and few other builders nearby, so the next gap between site contracts already worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the housing-site porch roofs and check AI board counts against the marked timber. We'll stop ordering takeaway meals for the next month and use those wages for the normal bills, while I ask the builder for the next paid job date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even if AI is modest. A faster AI timber list cannot cover a week between porch contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the contract gap hit the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the next site started four days late and the grocery rota was short too. The rent and food still landed on the same dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending would actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would cut the optional takeaway, not the grocery shop. The money stays available for rent; we are not calling the three-week reserve a new deposit.

say: **Porch roofs** remain physical carpentry despite quicker timber orders.
A modest tool does not resolve **gaps between site contracts**.
think: My **lead skill** still brings below-trade pay.
Three weeks of **savings** and variable grocery shifts make a contract gap serious.
do: **Finish** housing-site porch roofs and check AI board counts.
**Stop** optional takeaway meals next month to protect rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about existing income gaps even in a mild AI picture.
S0.quote: A faster AI timber list cannot cover a week between porch contracts.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** but knows faster ordering does not repair low pay or contract gaps.
Her **three-week reserve** and partner's variable grocery shifts make baseline anxiety credible despite high site skill.

steps.text: Finish housing-site porch roofs and check daily AI board counts
Stop optional takeaway meals next month to protect rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will handle ordering and schedules before a robot can brace a porch roof. A small builder should keep a real carpenter checking the measurements before the timber truck leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The computer might squeeze jobs into shorter paid days, and our thin reserve cannot carry many of those. I'm quick with new software, but being good at the job will not make a short pay packet longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll learn the new AI scheduling controls on the next empty porch bay and compare their planned hours with the last three jobs. If the office order cuts a crew day without a safe build plan, I'll show the numbers to the owner before work starts and ask for a full paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic cut to paid hours, though I can try the tool and argue from measurements. I will not let a tidy schedule put a worker on a roof without time to brace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before accepting a schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the brace positions on the drawing and compare them with the actual wall. A porch roof will not stand safely because the AI calendar says the crew is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the owner about paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring three payslips, the actual hours and the revised AI schedule to the owner. If the shorter days become policy, I will check the few local building vacancies before our reserve is gone.

say: **AI scheduling** may change before robots handle porch roofs.
A carpenter must check **safe bracing time** against the office plan.
think: My own **paid hours** could realistically shrink under a tighter schedule.
A **three-week reserve** leaves little room for several short shifts.
do: **Learn** AI scheduling controls on empty porch bay.
**Compare** planned hours with last three paid roof jobs.
**Ask** owner for full paid shift if AI order lacks safe build time.
feel: **Anxious** about shorter paid days, still able to test and challenge them.
S1.quote: A porch roof will not stand safely because the AI calendar says the crew is finished.
fieldNote: She learns **new AI controls** early, using actual payslips and brace measurements to challenge shortened shifts.
The prospect of **less paid time** directly threatens a household with less than a month saved.

steps.text: Learn AI scheduling controls on empty porch bay
Compare AI hours with three paid porch jobs
Ask owner for full paid shift when plan lacks safe build time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can plan the roof, and capable robots around 2031 could fit it. The builder must publish the paid crew rota before asking workers to trust a machine demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 63 when robots can do the physical work, and I have no affordable retirement date in hand. I expect our small builder to cut most porch shifts if the robot works; with three weeks saved and few local jobs, I have lain awake thinking about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the builder for a written staffing plan and a safe robot trial with a worker able to stop it. If a funded, recognised site-machine course offers a real place and full wages during class, I'll enrol; if porch shifts are cut, I'll apply only to posted local construction jobs with safe duties and pay that covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a major loss of shifts I think likely, and I have lost sleep over the rent. I can still take concrete steps, but our cash gives us almost no waiting time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the rent gets paid before we buy another tool. Our grown children have their own bills, so I will look for work first rather than count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe porch robot trial require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot should test on a braced ground-level mock porch with an exclusion zone and a worker who can cut power. A sales clip does not tell us whether the roof can carry its load.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans roofs before robots fit them around 2031.
The builder should publish **paid crew rotas** and safe trial rules.
think: At about **63**, I expect most porch shifts to vanish before retirement is affordable.
Three weeks of **savings** and few local jobs leave rent exposed.
do: **Ask** builder for written porch rota and protected stop-enabled robot trial.
**Enrol** in funded recognised site-machine course if real place and full class wages secured.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local construction job with safe rent-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major shift loss and sleepless rent worry, with a plan.
S2.quote: I expect our small builder to cut most porch shifts if the robot works; with three weeks saved and few local jobs, I have lain awake thinking about rent.
fieldNote: Her **expected major shift loss** and reported lost sleep meet the alarmed threshold, despite adaptive behaviour.
Training needs **funded fees**, a place and full wages; applications need cut shifts and posted local work with safe adequate pay.

steps.text: Ask builder for written porch rota and protected stop-enabled robot trial
Enrol in funded recognised site-machine course if real place and full class wages secured
Apply after cuts to posted local construction job with safe rent-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 could design the roof while robots around 2034 might brace it. Five years is enough to teach the next worker safe machine setup if a firm actually pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 66 when robots can do our site work. I hope to leave regular roofing around 69 if our income allows, so a cut at 66 would still leave years to fund, but the longer warning gives me a chance to build a little cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take the free evening machine-safety introduction at the trade centre this winter while I still earn a wage. If the builder funds a recognised equipment certificate, gives a real place and pays assessment days, I'll enrol next intake; I will also put twenty from each full paid week into a new reserve if rent and groceries are covered first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap near 66, but five years offers more control than two. I can start a free class without borrowing money for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety class need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the instructor to make me stop a machine when a brace is loose on a grounded frame. A site robot video cannot show me the feel of a loose porch brace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would new saving come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty would come from future full wages after rent and food, not money moved from the three-week reserve. If a short week leaves no spare pay, there is no deposit.

say: **2031 thinking AI** designs roofs before robots brace them around 2034.
A five-year lead permits **funded hands-on training** and a little new saving.
think: At about **66**, I may still need roofing wages until an affordable exit around 69.
A **thin reserve** makes any shift cut serious, though warning time helps.
do: **Attend** free evening machine-safety introduction while still employed.
**Enrol** in recognised equipment course if funded place and paid assessment days secured.
**Deposit** twenty from full paid week if rent and groceries covered.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible late-career wage gap, with time to prepare.
S3.quote: A site robot video cannot show me the feel of a loose porch brace.
fieldNote: She starts **actual free study** and keeps further certification conditional on funding, a real place and paid assessment days.
Her **new deposits** come only from future full wages after essentials, never from the existing three-week account.

steps.text: Attend free evening machine-safety introduction while employed
Enrol in recognised equipment course if funded place and paid assessment days secured
Deposit twenty from full paid week if rent and groceries covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may plan porch roofs and robots around 2039 may build them. A decade is enough for families and apprentices to learn a trade and a new tool together, if the paid work survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 71 when robots can do the physical work, beyond the age I hope to stop around 69. But with low pay and three weeks saved today, I cannot claim I'll be retired by then until actual income statements say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the present porch crew and ask the trade guild's apprenticeship group for paid ground-level machine lessons. My partner and I will review retirement income each year; if it is short and I still need a wage after 69, I'll apply only to posted local light-duty construction work with safe hours and pay that covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's thin account and uncertain retirement, even with a long robot runway. I can plan a safer handover, not promise an exit date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new porch fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a young fitter to find the brace that looks fine but moves under a pull. A robot's drawing will not protect a family beneath an untested porch roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the guild lesson safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guild lesson needs paid apprentice hours, a grounded frame and a named safety trainer. If those cannot be provided, I will not ask a beginner to practise beneath a raised roof.

say: **2036 thinking AI** plans roofs before robots build them around 2039.
**Paid safe apprenticeships** should teach real brace checks.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be off regular sites if retirement income permits.
Today's **low pay** and tiny reserve keep the household exposed now.
do: **Keep** leading present porch crew and checking roof braces.
**Ask** trade guild for paid supervised ground-level machine lesson.
**Apply** if income short after 69 to posted local light-duty job with safe rent-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about present cash and uncertain exit, despite more robot warning.
S4.quote: A robot's drawing will not protect a family beneath an untested porch roof.
fieldNote: She makes **2039 work conditional** on short retirement income and an actual posted safe local job.
The **guild apprenticeship proposal** includes paid time, ground-level practice and supervision rather than an unsafe informal lesson.

steps.text: Keep leading present porch crew and checking roof braces
Ask trade guild for paid supervised ground-level machine lesson
Apply if income short after 69 to posted local light-duty job with safe rent-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because porch robots around 2031 could wipe out paid shifts when I would be about 63, years before I can afford to stop. A written crew rota, funded full-wage training and real local jobs with safe duties and rent-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the carpenter when a robot supplier shows a flawless roof but our builder cuts the crew before a safe trial. A porch roof can pass a screen test and still need a hand on every brace. Rent comes due either way.

headlineQuote: A porch roof can pass a screen test and still need a hand on every brace.
portrait: **Aisha**, 58, leads porch-roof carpentry with a vocational certificate and strong skill despite below-trade pay.
She and her grocery-worker partner have a **three-week reserve**; grown children have their own bills and local building jobs are scarce.
She uses **AI daily**, learns new controls early and favours paid, supervised apprenticeships rooted in practical work.
Existing contract gaps make her **anxious**; fast robots alarm her because she expects major shift loss and reports sleeplessness.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring porch robots around 2031 when she would be about 63 and still need rent money.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew rota**, funded full-wage training and posted safe local work with rent-covering pay would help.
